scenes.title: Where do I put each capability

sentences.text: Multi-agent design answers one question: where do I put each capability?
Copilot Studio gives you child agents.
They live inside the same main agent.
They are lightweight, built for one use case and one team.
They have no settings, authentication, or deployment of their own, and they are not published separately.
Copilot Studio also offers connected agents.
These are other Copilot Studio agents in the same environment, each with its own publishing and life cycle.
The orchestrator of the main agent decides which one to hand work to, based on their descriptions.
You can also connect external agents through A two A, Microsoft Foundry, Fabric data agents, and the Microsoft three six five Agents S D K.
Start simple.
Split your agent when the accuracy of tool selection starts to drop.
As a rule of thumb, that happens with more than thirty to forty options across tools, topics, and agents, or when descriptions look alike.
Also split when there are several teams, different publishing channels, their own settings, independent A L M, or a need to reuse.
Splitting has a price.
Every extra orchestration hop adds latency.
It also makes the surface you must test and govern bigger.
So do not split without a reason.
A single agent that works well is better than many agents that are hard to test, slow to answer, and difficult to govern.
Think about Contoso.
Software licenses are handled by one team with one use case, so that goes in as a child agent.
Human resources has its own team, channels, and publishing, so it is a connected agent.
On the exam, justify your choice with team, A L M, publishing, and reuse.
